question: When fats become institutions — laws, sacrifices, gymnasia — which fat belongs to which civilisation?
summary: This is the period in which the olive becomes Greek, ghee becomes Indian and the northern butter becomes a mark of barbarism. At Ekron in Philistia a purpose-built quarter of over a hundred presses shows industrial oil in the 600s BC ([[ec1]]); in Athens an estimated 200–330 kg of olive oil a year goes through a wealthy household for food, lamps and the body ([[ec2]], [[te2]], [[te3]]), the Panathenaic prizes carry the goddess's oil ([[b3]]) and Solon is said to have let Attica export only oil ([[o1]]). The beam press is the Greek machine ([[te1]]).

India offers the contrasting culture: the Vedic sacrifice makes ghee a ‘commodity of enormous prestige’ ([[b1]]), sesame is one of the nine sacred grains ([[b2]]), and mustard and safflower are named as oil sources ([[ec3]]). Sesame also moves west and north, to Babylon's only oil in Herodotus ([[th1]]), a workshop at Karmir Blur ([[ec4]]) and a Macedonian tavern ([[ec5]]).

Between these oil cultures lies a fat frontier. A Greek comic poet mocks the Thracians as ‘butter eaters’ ([[e1]]); the Zhou court cooks each meat in its own animal fat, since no oil was pressed in China before the Han ([[th2]]); and the origin of the olive in Italy and the west is still argued ([[x1]]).

themes.title: The Greek olive: an economy and a body
text: Presses, consumption figures, lamps and the gymnasium show oil as food, light and cleanser at once, and Athena's trees make it sacred. Solon's export law is the earliest state measure on oil, but its authenticity is disputed.

themes.title: Industrial oil in the Near East
text: Ekron's hundred presses and Karmir Blur's sesame workshop are the largest known oil works of the Iron Age; Herodotus's Babylon uses sesame, not olive oil.

themes.title: India: ghee, sesame and the sacred
text: Ghee fries food and feeds the sacred fire; sesame is a sacred grain; oil is a growing alternative by the Sutra period.

themes.title: Where the frontier runs
text: Butter against oil in Greek comedy; animal fat against pressed oil in China; the olive's western spread.

turning_points.text: A sesame-oil workshop is built at Karmir Blur.
Solon allows only olive oil to be exported from Attica.
The beam press is the Greek machine for oil and wine.
Herodotus: the Babylonians use only sesame oil.
A Greek comedy calls the Thracians ‘butter eaters’.

how_to_read: Start with the Greek entries in *Economy* and *Technology*, which are the best-quantified in the folio, then *Belief* for the Indian ghee and sesame. The Nexus links the household oil figures to lamps, the gymnasium and the sacred.
China is the contrast: look at *Thought* for the Zhou fats before the next folio's first pressing of seeds.

sources.intro: The Greek half rests on one excellent book; the Indian and Chinese halves on a translated reference work each; the Near Eastern industrial sites on a journalist's summary and an atlas folio.
main: Foxhall, *Olive Cultivation in Ancient Greece*, for Athens, the press and the lamp ([[ec2]], [[te1]], [[te2]], [[te3]], [[b3]], [[o1]], [[x1]]).
Achaya, *Indian Food Tradition*, for ghee, sesame and mustard oil ([[b1]], [[b2]], [[ec3]]).
Needham, SCC 6.5, for the Zhou fats ([[th2]]); Bedigian for sesame in Babylon and Urartu ([[th1]], [[ec4]], [[ec5]]).
Mueller and the atlas folio on Philistia for Ekron ([[ec1]]); Khosrova for the butter eaters ([[e1]]).
contested: Solon's law ([[o1]]) and the question of who brought the olive west ([[x1]]).
The Athenian household figures are an estimate, not a record ([[ec2]]).
The Zhou li passage was compiled later than the period it describes ([[th2]]).
gaps: Phoenician and Carthaginian roles in spreading the olive are not covered; nor is Egypt's own oil economy under the Ptolemies (see the next folio).
The Indian texts were read only through Achaya, and Chinese oils only through Needham.
